subtitle: Plan a reorganization, reassignment or layoff so you can show who bears its effects, work within seniority and contract rules, keep accommodations in place, communicate fairly and check the result afterward.
audience: For DHS and DSD managers, program managers, senior leaders and supervisors who design or carry out reorganizations, reassignments or reductions, and for the staff who advise them. It builds on the supervisor course on budget cuts, reassignment and separation.

lessons.title: Who bears the impact
objectives: Map the direct and second-order effects of a proposed workforce change before names are attached.
Identify groups of positions and employees who may bear concentrated effects, such as recent hires, people on leave, people with accommodations and staff in language access or community roles.
Use the State of Minnesota Equity Analysis Toolkit questions to plan an impact review with a decision owner.
Handle workforce data with attention to small numbers, confidentiality and privacy.
lessons.teaching:
A reorganization usually begins as a picture of functions and boxes. People experience it as a change to their caseload, their supervisor, their location, their schedule or their job itself. The supervisor course on budget cuts, reassignment and separation covers a supervisor's input and the hard conversations. This course is for the people who design the change. The first discipline is the same one used in hiring: describe the functions and the reasons for the change before thinking about who holds each position. The second belongs to this level: before the design is final, map who would bear its effects and how those effects add up.

Direct effects are the obvious ones: positions eliminated, duties moved, reporting lines changed. Second-order effects are easier to miss. A change of location can fall hardest on employees with disabilities, caregivers or people who live far from the new site. A rule that follows hire date can concentrate losses among recent hires, who may include people brought in through recent recruitment for skills the program said it needed. Cutting functions labeled non-core can remove community engagement or language access work, the people who do it and the service families relied on. Moving a team to a new system or supervisor can interrupt accommodations that were working. Employees on leave can be missed in both planning and communication. None of these is a finding about DSD. They are questions a design team should be able to answer before a decision is made.

The State of Minnesota Equity Analysis Toolkit offers a structure built on plain questions: what outcomes are intended, who is included, how to collaborate, what impact will result, how to be accountable and how to communicate. Apply it to the design rather than to individual employees. Ask which groups of positions are affected, what work and services would be lost or moved, and which effects a different design, phasing or support could reduce. Ask the people who would experience the change, including county and community partners where services cross into their work, what the design misses. Record who owns the decision and when it will be reviewed. An impact review without an owner tends to become a document that arrives after the decision.

Workforce data needs care. Counts in a single unit are often small enough that a table by race, disability or age identifies individuals. Accommodation and medical information is confidential and is not a planning input for managers. Ask Human Resources what aggregated information can be shared, with whom and at what level, and let Human Resources run any analysis that requires personnel data. A pattern in the projected effects is a reason to revisit the design or ask more questions. It is never a reason to change one person's outcome because of a protected trait. Formal decisions about positions, layoffs, reassignments and accommodations stay with Human Resources, labor relations, the ADA coordinator and the leaders authorized to make them; this course helps you prepare the questions those decisions depend on.
lessons.keyPoint: Map who would bear a change's effects, including second-order effects, before the design is final. A pattern is a reason to revisit the design, never a reason to change one person's outcome because of a protected trait.
lessons.example: Practice case: {{PROGRAM_MANAGER}} is leading the design of a reorganization that would merge two units and move the merged team to a different site. The draft plan lists functions, positions and a new reporting structure. {{SUPERVISOR}} points out that the plan says nothing about who would be affected by the site change or what happens to the community liaison work one of the units does.
lessons.question: What should {{PROGRAM_MANAGER}} do before the plan goes to leadership?
choices: Send the plan forward now and offer to collect concerns from affected staff after the announcement.
Add an impact review of the site change and the liaison work, using aggregated data from HR.
Ask each supervisor for a list of employees likely to struggle with the move, with reasons.
feedback: Collecting concerns after the announcement turns design problems into individual complaints and makes changes harder to make. Effects that can be foreseen should shape the plan.

This examines the design's effects while the design can still change, keeps personnel and medical information with Human Resources, and gives leadership a plan that shows what the change would cost and for whom.

This asks supervisors to speculate about individuals and may draw out health or family information that does not belong in planning. Review the design's effects on groups of positions and services instead.
lessons.reflection: Privately recall a reorganization you lived through or helped lead, or use the practice case. Which effects were foreseen, which surprised people, and who ended up carrying the surprises?
lessons.action: For a change your area is considering, list the functions affected and write one possible second-order effect for each: location, schedule, accommodation, language access, community relationships or workload. Note who owns the decision and when it will be reviewed.

check.question: Why should an impact review come before a reorganization design is final?
check.correct: So effects that can be foreseen can still shape the design, phasing or support.
wrong: So managers can adjust individual outcomes based on employees' protected traits.
So the review can replace the contract's rules on layoff and reassignment.
check.feedback: An early review lets the design change while it still can. It never authorizes changing one person's outcome because of a protected trait, and it works within the contract's rules rather than replacing them.

lessons.title: Seniority, contracts and equity goals
objectives: Explain where layoff and reassignment rules for state employees come from, including contracts and compensation plans.
Describe how Title VII treats bona fide seniority systems and disparate impact, and why current enforcement questions go to legal counsel.
Identify decisions made before seniority applies where equity analysis can still shape who is affected.
Bring labor relations a question that keeps both the contract and equity goals in view.
lessons.teaching:
For most state employees, the order in which people are laid off, displaced or recalled is not a manager's choice. Minnesota Statutes section 43A.07 refers to the layoff provisions of compensation plans and of collective bargaining agreements, and those agreements and plans set the rules for the employees they cover. Contracts and plans differ in how they treat seniority, layoff units, bumping, recall and reassignment, so the first question for any change is which agreement or plan covers each affected position and what it says. Labor relations answers that question. Under Minnesota Statutes section 179A.07, a public employer is not required to negotiate inherent managerial policy, which includes matters such as its functions and programs, overall budget, organizational structure and the selection and direction of personnel, but it must meet and negotiate in good faith on terms and conditions of employment. Where that line falls in a particular change is also a labor relations question.

Federal law gives seniority systems a specific status. Section 703(h) of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 says it is not an unlawful employment practice to apply different standards or terms under a bona fide seniority system, provided the differences are not the result of an intention to discriminate. Title VII also contains a disparate-impact provision, section 703(k), which sets out how a claim about a practice with unequal effects is proved and defended. How federal agencies enforce disparate-impact theories has shifted recently, and Minnesota law has its own prohibitions, so ask legal counsel what applies now rather than relying on a summary. The practical point does not depend on that answer. A leader cannot set aside a contract's seniority order to protect a group, and choosing who stays or goes because of a protected trait would raise its own legal problem. Equity goals have to work through the design, not around the rules.

There is more room than it first appears, because many decisions come before seniority applies. Which functions are reduced, which positions and classes are affected, whether the change is phased, whether vacancies are held for affected staff, whether voluntary options or retraining are offered, and how the plan relates to the layoff units the contract defines can all change who is affected. These are the choices an impact review should inform. If cutting one function would remove most of a program's language access capacity, the equity question is whether that function should be cut, not who should be exempted from seniority. Some of these choices may themselves require notice or negotiation, which is one more reason to bring labor relations in early.

Seniority reflects values that employees and unions have bargained for, including predictability and protection from favoritism. It can also carry forward the effects of past hiring patterns. Both can be true, and an advanced leader holds them together without treating either as the whole story. Bring labor relations a specific question: here is the change, here are the positions affected, here is the effect we projected and here are the design options we are weighing. That gives labor relations what it needs to tell you what the contract allows and what must be negotiated or noticed.
lessons.keyPoint: Seniority and layoff rules come from contracts and plans, and labor relations interprets them. Equity analysis does its work in the decisions made before seniority applies: which functions, positions, phasing and supports the change includes.
lessons.example: Practice case: A reduction will eliminate several positions in one classification, and under the contract the order follows seniority. {{PROGRAM_MANAGER}} notices that most of the least senior employees in that class were hired in a recent recruitment for bilingual county liaison work. {{COMMUNITY_PARTNER}} has asked whether the county liaison role will survive the reduction.
lessons.question: What is the strongest next step for {{PROGRAM_MANAGER}}?
choices: Ask labor relations whether the newest liaison staff can be exempted from seniority to keep the work.
Apply the seniority order as written and tell the county partner the liaison role is not the program's concern.
Ask labor relations what the contract allows, and review whether the liaison function should be cut at all.
feedback: Asking is better than acting alone, but the question is framed as an exemption for particular people. The stronger question is about the function and the design, which is where the program has room.
Following the contract is right, but the function question is still open. Losing the liaison work affects the people the program serves, and the county partner's question deserves a real answer.
This respects the contract, gets an authoritative answer about what it allows, and moves the equity question to a decision the program controls: whether the liaison function should be reduced.
lessons.reflection: Privately consider what seniority protects for the people you work with, and what it might carry forward. How would you explain both to a colleague who sees only one side?
lessons.action: Find the layoff, seniority and reassignment provisions in the contract or plan that covers positions in your area. List the decisions in a change that would come before those provisions apply, and write one question for labor relations.

check.question: Under Title VII section 703(h), when is applying different terms under a seniority system protected?
check.correct: When the system is bona fide and the differences are not the result of an intention to discriminate.
wrong: Whenever the system was negotiated with a union, regardless of its purpose or history.
Only when the employer can show the system has no unequal effect on any group.
check.feedback: Section 703(h) protects bona fide seniority systems as long as the differences do not result from an intention to discriminate. Whether another theory or Minnesota law reaches a particular practice is a question for legal counsel.

lessons.title: Accommodations through a change
objectives: Explain why the duty to provide reasonable accommodation continues through reorganizations, reassignments and new systems.
Plan for accommodation continuity when duties, supervisors, locations or technology change.
Describe how EEOC guidance treats reassignment as an accommodation, including its interaction with seniority systems.
Keep medical information confidential while planning a change.
lessons.teaching:
A reorganization can undo accommodations without anyone deciding to. An approved schedule, a piece of assistive technology, a workspace arrangement or a way of receiving assignments may depend on a particular supervisor, site or system. When those change, the accommodation can quietly disappear. The course on accommodation transitions addresses the handoff for one person. At the design level, the question is whether the change plan itself treats accommodation as something to carry forward. The EEOC's enforcement guidance on reasonable accommodation and undue hardship, issued in 2002 and noting that later amendments broadened the definition of disability, describes the duty to accommodate as ongoing: an employee may need different accommodations at different times, and if one stops being effective, the employer must consider an alternative.

Minnesota Management and Budget HR/LR Policy 1433 has each agency head appoint an ADA coordinator, who decides requests outside supervisors' authority and must be consulted before any denial. The policy calls for an interactive process when a need or limitation is unclear or a medical condition changes, and it requires medical information to be kept separate and confidential, with supervisors learning only the work restrictions and accommodations they need to know. For a change plan, that means three things. Ask the ADA coordinator early to help identify, without sharing medical details with planners, which approved accommodations may be affected by new duties, locations, schedules or systems. Build time and budget for continuing or adjusting them into the plan. And tell every affected employee how to raise an access need about the change, without requiring anyone to disclose a condition.

Reassignment is where accommodation and workforce change meet most directly. The EEOC guidance calls reassignment to a vacant position the accommodation of last resort, required when no accommodation would let the employee perform the essential functions of the current job or when every other option would cause undue hardship. A qualified employee does not have to compete for a vacant position at the same level, but must compete for one that would be a promotion. The guidance also says that, after the Supreme Court's decision in US Airways v. Barnett, reassignment that would violate a seniority system is generally unreasonable, with an exception where special circumstances undermine employees' expectations of uniform treatment. Policy 1433 has the ADA coordinator, working with Human Resources, look first at equivalent vacancies and then at lower-level ones. During a reduction, vacancies may be scarce and claimed under the contract, so these questions need the ADA coordinator, Human Resources and labor relations working together.

The edge cases are real. An employee whose position is eliminated may also have a pending accommodation request, and that request still needs an answer. A new system chosen for a merged unit may not work with assistive technology someone already uses; that is a design flaw to raise before purchase, not after go-live. A return to a site may conflict with an approved telework accommodation; that conflict goes to the ADA coordinator, not to a blanket rule. In each case the planner's job is to surface the question early and route it, so that the change does not become the reason an accommodation lapses.
lessons.keyPoint: The duty to accommodate continues through a change. Plan for it with the ADA coordinator, keep medical information out of planning, and bring reassignment questions to the ADA coordinator, Human Resources and labor relations together.
lessons.example: Practice case: A merged unit will move to a new case management system and a new site in three months. {{SUPERVISOR}} knows that two team members have approved accommodations but not the details. {{NEW_COLLEAGUE}}, who is helping with the transition plan, suggests a shared spreadsheet listing each employee's accommodation so the move can be planned around them.
lessons.question: How should {{SUPERVISOR}} respond?
choices: Ask the ADA coordinator to review affected accommodations and tell everyone how to raise access needs.
Build the spreadsheet, but limit access to the transition team so medical details stay protected there.
Wait until after the move, then ask the two employees whether their accommodations still work.
feedback: This keeps medical information with the person responsible for it, gets affected accommodations reviewed before the move, and gives every employee a way to raise a need, including people whose needs no one on the team knows about.

Limiting access helps, but a planning spreadsheet of accommodations still moves confidential information outside the ADA coordinator and Human Resources. The plan needs to know what to carry forward, not why.
Checking in afterward is good practice, but by then a lapse may already have happened. The system and the site are known now, so the review can happen now.
lessons.reflection: Privately think about an accommodation you know of, your own or one you supported, that depended on a particular person, place or system. What would have protected it through a change?
lessons.action: Add an accommodation continuity step to a change plan you are part of: a date to consult the ADA coordinator, a budget line for adjustments, and a message telling every affected employee how to raise an access need.

check.question: According to EEOC guidance, how is reassignment to a vacant position treated as an accommodation?
check.correct: As the accommodation of last resort, when no accommodation in the current job would be effective.
wrong: As the first option to offer whenever a job changes in a reorganization.
As a promotion the employee may claim without competing for it.
check.feedback: The guidance calls reassignment the accommodation of last resort. A qualified employee need not compete for a vacant position at the same level but must compete for a promotion, and reassignment that would violate a seniority system is generally unreasonable unless special circumstances apply.

lessons.title: Communicating fairly and checking the result
objectives: Plan communication about a workforce change so people affected in the same way get the same accurate information in usable forms.
Identify information that needs particular care, including federal requirements for age-related waivers that Human Resources and legal counsel manage.
Design a review after the change that compares actual effects with the projected ones.
Report back to employees and partners without overclaiming success.
lessons.teaching:
Fair communication during workforce change is mostly about sameness and timing. People affected in the same way should learn the same facts at about the same time, from someone accountable, in a form they can use. Quiet early warnings to trusted staff, which the supervisor course on budget cuts warns against, give some people an advantage and tend to follow existing relationships. Plan the sequence with Human Resources and labor relations, because contracts and plans may require notice to employees or the union before certain changes, and the timing and content of that notice are theirs to confirm. Make materials accessible, offer interpretation or translation where staff need it, include employees who are on leave, and give everyone the same route for questions.

Some information needs particular care. What can be said about an individual's position or departure depends on personnel data rules, so ask Human Resources before describing why anyone left. If an agency offers separation agreements that include a release of claims as part of a group program, federal law adds requirements for employees age 40 and older. The EEOC's question-and-answer guidance explains that in an exit incentive or other group termination program, employees must have at least 45 days to consider the waiver and seven days to revoke it after signing, and must receive written information about the decisional unit, the eligibility factors and time limits, the job titles and ages of those eligible or selected, and the ages of those in the same job classifications or unit who were not. That guidance was issued in 2009, so Human Resources and legal counsel should confirm current requirements. The disclosure itself is a reminder that federal law expects a group separation to be explainable by who was chosen and who was not.

The work does not end on the effective date. Plan a review at a point the change plan names in advance, and return to the impact map from the design stage. Did effects fall where they were projected? Which surprised people? Are accommodations working in the new structure? Did language access, community liaison or other functions survive in practice or only on the chart? Has workload for remaining staff grown, and on whom? Are complaints, grievances or departures concentrated anywhere? Human Resources should run any analysis that uses personnel data, with attention to small numbers. Seek the views of employees and partners, such as counties, who lived through the change, and give them a way to answer without being identified.

Report what the review found, including what did not work, and what will happen next. A finding of a barrier should lead to a decision with an owner and a date, such as restoring a function, adjusting workloads or repairing an accommodation process. It should not lead to reversing an individual decision because of a person's group, and it should not claim success because a plan's tasks were completed. A concern that a decision was made because of a protected trait is not a review finding to hold for later; it goes promptly to the person or area responsible, such as the Equal Opportunity and Access Division or Human Resources. Fairness in a change is something a leader can show afterward, not only intend beforehand.
lessons.keyPoint: Tell people affected in the same way the same facts at the same time, in usable forms. Then return to the impact map, report what you find, and act on barriers with an owner and a date.
lessons.example: Practice case: Four months after a reorganization, {{PROGRAM_MANAGER}} is asked to report to leadership on how it went. The positions are filled, the new structure is in place and the transition plan's tasks are complete. {{COMMUNITY_PARTNER}} has mentioned that families who relied on the former liaison now wait longer for callbacks, and several remaining staff have taken on extra duties.
lessons.question: What should the report to leadership include?
choices: A summary showing that every task in the transition plan was completed on time and the new structure is in place.
A comparison of actual and projected effects, including callback delays and workload, with owners for next steps.
A recommendation to wait a year before reviewing, since early problems often settle once people adjust to change.
feedback: Completing the plan is worth reporting, but it measures activity, not effect. Leadership would not learn about the callback delays or the shift in workload.
This returns to the impact map, uses what the county partner and staff observed, and turns findings into decisions with owners. It reports problems without treating them as failure.
Some problems do settle, but families are waiting now and remaining staff are carrying extra work. A review can note what may settle and still act on what will not.
lessons.reflection: Privately recall how you learned about a workforce change, as an employee or as a leader. What made the communication feel fair or unfair, and what would you repeat or avoid?
lessons.action: Write a one-page review plan for a change you are involved in: the review date, the effects you projected, the questions you will ask, who runs any analysis of personnel data, how employees and partners can respond, and how you will report back.

check.question: For a group termination program that offers waivers to employees age 40 and older, what does EEOC guidance say employees must receive?
check.correct: At least 45 days to consider, seven days to revoke, and written information on who was and was not selected.
wrong: At least 21 days to consider and a spoken explanation of how employees were selected.
A summary of the selection criteria, with ages reported in broad bands such as 40 to 50.
check.feedback: For group programs the guidance describes a 45-day consideration period, a seven-day revocation period and written disclosures, including job titles and ages of those selected and the ages of those not selected. Age bands do not meet the requirement. Human Resources and legal counsel confirm current rules.

cards.back: An effect of a change beyond its stated purpose, such as a site move falling hardest on employees with long commutes, caregiving duties or approved accommodations.
A record, made before the design is final, of which functions, positions and services a change affects and how the effects add up. It is checked again after the change.

Rules on layoff order, bumping, recall and reassignment set by the collective bargaining agreement or compensation plan that covers a position. Contracts and plans differ; labor relations interprets them.

Matters such as functions, programs, budget, organizational structure and the selection and direction of personnel that a public employer need not negotiate under section 179A.07. Terms and conditions of employment must be negotiated.
Under Title VII section 703(h), applying different terms under one is lawful if the differences are not the result of an intention to discriminate.
Planning with the ADA coordinator so approved accommodations survive new duties, supervisors, sites or systems, without sharing medical details with planners.
The accommodation of last resort in EEOC guidance. Reassignment that would violate a seniority system is generally unreasonable unless special circumstances apply.

aid.heading: Before the design is final
items: Describe functions and reasons before positions and names.
Map direct and second-order effects: location, schedule, accommodations, language access and workload.
Name the decision owner and the review date.
Let Human Resources run any analysis that uses personnel data.

aid.heading: Work with the rules
items: Identify the contract or plan that covers each affected position.
Ask labor relations what the layoff and reassignment provisions require and what must be negotiated or noticed.
Put equity analysis into decisions made before seniority applies.
Never adjust an individual's outcome because of a protected trait.

aid.heading: Carry access forward
items: Consult the ADA coordinator early about accommodations the change may affect.
Budget time and money for continuing or adjusting them.
Tell every affected employee how to raise an access need.
Bring reassignment questions to the ADA coordinator, HR and labor relations together.

aid.heading: Communicate and check
items: Give people affected in the same way the same facts at the same time, in usable forms.
Include employees on leave and confirm required notice with HR and labor relations.
Compare actual effects with the impact map and report back with owners and dates.
Route concerns about protected traits promptly to the person or area responsible.

sources.title: Minnesota Statutes section 43A.07 — Classified service
sources.note: Subdivision 4 refers to the layoff provisions of compensation plans and collective bargaining agreements (lesson 2). It does not state any layoff order; the applicable contract or plan does.

sources.title: Minnesota Statutes section 179A.07 — Employer rights and obligations
sources.note: Supports the description of inherent managerial policy and the duty to meet and negotiate on terms and conditions of employment (lesson 2). Where a particular change falls is a question for labor relations.

sources.title: U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission — Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964
sources.note: Statutory text for section 703(h) on bona fide seniority systems and section 703(k) on disparate impact (lesson 2). Current federal enforcement positions were not reviewed for this course; ask legal counsel.

sources.title: U.S. EEOC — Enforcement Guidance on Reasonable Accommodation and Undue Hardship under the ADA
sources.note: Supports the ongoing duty to accommodate, reassignment as the accommodation of last resort, competition for promotions, and the treatment of seniority systems after US Airways v. Barnett (lesson 3). Issued 2002; it notes that later amendments broadened the definition of disability.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — HR/LR Policy 1433, ADA Reasonable Accommodations
sources.note: Supports the ADA coordinator's role, the interactive process, confidentiality of medical information and the order for considering vacancies in reassignment (lesson 3). The version read lists its latest revision in 2017.

sources.title: U.S. EEOC — Understanding Waivers of Discrimination Claims in Employee Severance Agreements
sources.note: Supports the 45-day consideration period, seven-day revocation period and written disclosures for group programs involving employees age 40 and older (lesson 4). Issued 2009; Human Resources and legal counsel confirm current requirements.
